cards.title: Room theft report
steps: Go to the guest. Apologise for the situation, not for fault. Take a full statement with open questions and a timeline.
Offer to help the guest report it to the police. Never discourage a report.
Look and photograph: door, frame, lock, safe, balcony. Touch as little as possible.
Interrogate the lock: download and print the audit trail.
Check the keycard encoding log for duplicate keys and the lost property log for the item.
Interview every member of staff whose key appears, the same shift, with open questions, after you know what the lock says.
Review CCTV for the times the evidence points to; export the clips with a hash and a custody record.
Log every item of evidence into the LP locker. Release property only after ownership is proven, with a signature.
Report the facts; brief the duty manager; liability and compensation go to claims and the GM, never decided on the floor.
cards.why: A theft claim is a claim, not a fact. The objective evidence (lock, cameras, logs) protects the guest who is right and the employee who is innocent.
pitfalls: Searching or accusing staff on a hunch
Promising compensation
Watching footage without exporting it

cards.title: Writing the incident report
steps: Who: everyone involved, with role and how you identified them.
What: what happened, in one factual line, then the detail.
When and where: times from systems (locks, cameras, logs), not memory, and exact places.
How: what the evidence shows, with references (photo, export, log numbers).
Actions: what you did, in order, and who you told.
Facts, not opinions: write what you saw and heard. Quote people; do not characterise them.
Note where a statement and the evidence differ, without judging the person.
cards.why: Your report may be read by the GM, an insurer, the police or a court, months later. Only facts survive that reading.
pitfalls: Opinions about guests or staff
Vague lines with no times or references
Leaving out an inconvenient fact

cards.title: Identity check before room entry
steps: Never open a guest room, or give out a room number, until identity is verified against the registration.
Ask for photo ID and match the name to the registered guest or a registered sharer.
No ID: verify through the registration details only the guest would know, or call the registered guest.
If the person is not registered, do not confirm or deny who is staying in the room.
If the registered guest asks not to be disturbed, respect it, and stay with the visitor until they leave or the situation is resolved.
Record the request, the checks and the outcome in the daily activity report.
cards.why: Letting the wrong person into a room is one of the most serious failures a hotel can make. It can put a guest in real danger.
pitfalls: Opening the door because the person seems confident
Confirming a guest is staying
Arguing with an upset visitor instead of de-escalating

cards.title: Noise complaint and de-escalation
steps: Get the complaint details: who, which room, how long, what kind of noise.
Go in pairs. Tell the night manager where you are going.
Listen at the door first. Note what you hear and the time.
Knock, identify yourself, stand to the side of the door, and ask the guest to step into the doorway. Do not enter.
Calm voice, open hands, explain the problem and what you need. Give a clear, polite request and a time.
Watch for safety issues: overcrowding, smoke detectors covered, intoxication, anyone at risk.
Follow the warning policy. Eviction is the night manager's decision, under policy and local law.
Follow up with the complainant and record every visit and time.
cards.why: Most noise complaints end with one polite knock. The ones that escalate do so because staff argued, entered, or threatened what they could not deliver.
pitfalls: Going alone
Entering the room
Threatening eviction you have no authority to carry out

cards.title: Intoxicated guest: welfare first
steps: Ask the server what was served, over how long, and whether anything else was taken (medication, drugs).
Check welfare: responds to voice, breathing, colour, injuries, ability to walk. Never leave the person alone.
Call an ambulance at once for any red flag: hard to wake, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, a head injury, alcohol mixed with medication with worsening signs.
Back any refusal of service calmly; offer water; never shame the guest or the server.
Verify identity against the registration and the ID on file before any key or door.
Escort with two staff, stay at the threshold, leave them settled with water and a light on.
Go back to check (about 30 minutes), log each check with the time, and brief the night manager.
cards.why: Most alcohol deaths in hotels happen after the person has been put to bed and left alone. Supervision and a recheck cost minutes.
pitfalls: Treating it as a security problem
Making a key because it is obviously them
Escorting alone or entering the room
No recheck

cards.title: Collapse: call, push, shock
steps: Check response (voice, firm tap) and breathing for no more than ten seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing.
Send someone to call the emergency number on speaker and someone for the nearest AED.
Start chest compressions: centre of the chest, about two a second, five to six centimetres deep, full recoil. Do not stop except for the AED.
Switch the AED on and follow its prompts. Nobody touches the patient while it analyses or shocks.
Open the route: unlock doors, staff at the kerb to guide the crew, a lift held, furniture moved, onlookers kept back.
Hand over clearly: time of collapse, what was done, shocks given, medical history and medication.
Afterwards: restock and self-test the AED, log its use, look after the staff who helped, share health details on a need-to-know basis.
cards.why: Every minute without CPR and defibrillation costs about a tenth of the chance of survival. The first five minutes belong to the people already there.
pitfalls: Mistaking gasping for breathing
Waiting for the ambulance before starting compressions
Moving the patient out of sight
Locked doors at night
An AED put back without pads

cards.title: Unattended item: assess before you touch
steps: Ask who found it, when, and whether anyone has touched it.
Assess from a distance against three questions: is it hidden, is it obviously suspicious (wires, liquids, smell, sound), is it typical for the place and time?
Do not touch, move or open it, and keep radios and mobile phones a safe distance away until it is assessed.
Use CCTV and the front office to find who left it and why.
Hidden, suspicious or unexplained: clear the area, keep people back, call the police, follow the bomb threat and evacuation plan.
Typical and explained: move it with a witness, tag it, enter it in the lost property register and lock it away.
Contact the owner and let them describe the contents.
cards.why: Most unattended items are forgotten luggage, which is exactly why staff handle them casually. The assessment protects everyone if it is real, and the hotel from needless evacuations and complaints if it is not.
pitfalls: Carrying it to the desk
Opening it to find a name
Radios used beside it
Evacuating on time alone, without an assessment

cards.title: Preserving CCTV evidence
steps: Note exactly what is asked for: cameras, date, time window, and who is asking.
Check the recorder's retention and work out when the footage overwrites. That is your deadline.
Review first, then export wide: before and after the event, and every camera on the route in and out.
Export in the recorder's native format with its player, record the hash, and use write-once media where you have it.
Use your own login. Never a shared account.
Log the export (reason, cameras, times, format, media number, hash, witness) and lock the media in the evidence locker.
Preserve for anyone who asks; release only under the footage release policy, decided by the Director of LP and counsel where needed.
cards.why: Footage overwrites in weeks and requests arrive late. An export that cannot be attributed or verified can be challenged; footage released casually can be a privacy breach.
pitfalls: Waiting for paperwork while the footage overwrites
A few seconds converted to MP4
The shared admin login
Emailing clips to whoever asks

cards.title: Lost or stolen master key
steps: Void an electronic master the moment it is reported. Investigate after; if it turns up, a new card costs nothing.
Pull the lock audit for that card: every door it touched since it was last seen in safe hands.
Check the rooms it opened or tried, and agree with the duty manager how and when affected guests are told.
Review CCTV on the floor and the routes off it: lifts and stairs.
Check the key log: who signed it out, when, and whether anything else on the same ring is missing.
Fix mechanical keys in proportion to what they open: re-core the locks that key fits, not the whole system.
Report theft or attempted entry to the police and preserve the audit and the footage.
Coach the employee: keys stay on the person, and reporting fast is thanked, never punished.
cards.why: A master card is a key to every guest on its floors, and the minutes between loss and void are the dangerous ones. Staff only report quickly when reporting is safe for them.
pitfalls: Searching for an hour before voiding
Calling it lost without asking the locks
Re-keying everything, or nothing
Waking guests at midnight to tell them
Blaming the attendant so the next loss goes unreported

cards.title: Door alarms and propped doors
steps: Respond in person to every door alarm. Acknowledging it on the panel is not a response.
Close and secure the door. Note what was holding it and who was nearby.
Sweep the area behind the door before anything else: assume someone came in until you know they did not.
Check what the door protects: stock, cages, offices, stairs.
Review the cameras for the whole time the door was open, and how anyone who came in left.
Read the alarm history. A repeating alarm is a process failure; find out why the door is being propped.
Fix the cause, and give staff a safe way to work until it is fixed.
Log every alarm with its cause, and review the log weekly.
cards.why: Exterior doors are the perimeter. Most are propped for convenience, and an alarm that is cleared without a response teaches the whole team that the door does not matter.
pitfalls: Clearing the alarm from the screen
Reviewing video before sweeping
Blaming the person and leaving the cause
Turning the alarm down instead of fixing the door

cards.title: Luggage room control
steps: Tag every bag with a two-part ticket: one half on the bag, one to the guest. Log the tag, name, description and time.
Keep the luggage room locked; sign its key out and back.
Release only against the guest's half of the ticket, and collect it.
No ticket: photo ID matching the name on the tag and a description of the bag. Log the proof seen.
A missing bag: search the room, read the tag book, talk to whoever released it, then review the cameras.
Report a theft quickly with any vehicle or route details, and preserve the footage.
Look after the guest's immediate needs within your authority; route the claim to the GM and the insurer.
cards.why: Property the hotel takes into its care is the hotel's responsibility, and names and tag numbers are easy to read in a busy lobby.
pitfalls: Releasing on a name and a number
An unlocked luggage room
Hiding behind a liability notice
Promising compensation you do not decide

cards.title: Auditing the key system
steps: Check every encoder against the asset register: model, serial, location.
Open the lock system's list of trusted encoders. A device the system trusts is a key factory, wherever it is.
Audit lock system accounts against the staff list: shared logins, leavers, and who holds admin rights.
Compare encodings with the front desk's encoding log; list every card no one can account for.
Export, hash and log the system evidence before changing any setting.
Close the gap the same night: remove rogue devices, disable shared and leavers' accounts, re-key affected occupied rooms.
Report to the system's owner and the Director of LP; the vendor and the police take it from there.
cards.why: Locks do what the system tells them. Shared logins make every change anonymous, and one extra trusted encoder undoes every other key control.
pitfalls: Counting the devices on the desk and stopping
Changing settings before exporting the evidence
Leaving a rogue device live to catch someone
Naming a suspect in an audit report

cards.title: Fire alarm: the first ten minutes
steps: Read the panel: which device, which zone, what time.
Call the fire authority at once. Do not wait to find out whether it is real.
Send a trained person to the device by the stairs. Never open a warm door; feel it with the back of the hand.
Evacuate the alarm zone under the phased plan; tell other floors what is happening and what to do.
Get the rooming list and the list of guests who need help; use refuges and tell the crew where people are.
Meet the crew at the fire command centre with the plans, the fire master keys and the facts.
Only the fire authority silences and resets the panel.
Account for every guest, then log the event with the panel print-out and the incident number.
cards.why: Fire spreads in minutes and hotel guests are sleeping strangers in an unfamiliar building. The plan's order means nobody spends those minutes deciding.
pitfalls: Investigating before calling
Opening a warm door
Resetting the panel to stop the noise
Evacuating everyone, or no one
Forgetting guests who need help

cards.title: Sprinkler impairment and fire watch
steps: Treat every impairment as a permit LP owns: what, where, how long, who.
Before the valve is closed, notify the fire authority and the insurer, and tell the front office.
Tag the closed valve and the panel with the permit number. Acknowledge the supervisory signal; never isolate the alarm.
Suspend hot work in the impaired area and stage extra extinguishers.
Set a dedicated fire watch: the whole area, at least hourly, logged, with nothing else to do.
If the job runs long, tell everyone the new time and keep the watch going with relief.
Restore: valve open and locked, main drain test witnessed, tags removed.
Tell everyone you told at the start; file the permit, the watch log and the test result.
cards.why: Fire losses cluster around protection that was out of service. A few quiet hours without sprinklers is exactly when nobody expects a fire.
pitfalls: Closing the valve first and telling people later
A fire watch with three other jobs
Forgetting the insurer
Leaving the valve shut or untested

cards.title: Guest injury and the claim that follows
steps: Person first: go to the guest, ask what hurts, give first aid and offer an ambulance. Record the offer and the answer.
Make the area safe with cones straight away, but photograph it before anyone cleans or moves anything.
Photograph wide, medium and close, with a scale in the frame; note lighting, mats, signage and footwear without judging.
Take signed statements from witnesses and staff in their own words, before they talk among themselves.
Preserve the CCTV for the whole approach, the fall and the response, and log the export.
Pull the cleaning and inspection logs for that area and that hour.
Show care without admitting fault: no promises to pay, no blame, no guesses about cause.
Give the insurer first notice the same day with the facts, the photos and the statements.
Fix the cause, and record what you changed and when.
cards.why: Most injury claims are won or lost on what was recorded in the first hour. Care for the guest and good evidence are the same job, and a careless promise at the scene can cost more than the injury.
pitfalls: Mopping before the photos
Promising the hotel will pay
Statements taken days later
Forgetting the inspection log

cards.title: Hot work permit
steps: No permit, no flame: welding, cutting, brazing and grinding need a signed permit before work starts.
Walk the area with the contractor: combustibles moved 11 m away or covered with fire blankets, openings and drains covered.
Check the contractor's insurance, competence and a charged extinguisher at the work point.
Isolate only the detectors in that zone, through the permit, with the fire panel log and the front office told. Never isolate more than the work needs.
Post a trained fire watch during the work and for at least 30 to 60 minutes after it ends, with a final check later.
Restore the detectors when the watch ends, test them and sign the permit closed.
File the permit and the watch log.
cards.why: Hot work fires often start in hidden places and smoulder long after the contractor has packed up, which is why the watch continues after the flame stops.
pitfalls: Isolating a whole floor of detectors
Ending the fire watch when the torch goes off
No extinguisher at the work
Leaving detectors isolated overnight
